newsitem.title: USA: At Home seen making big stock market splash.
newsitem.headline: At Home seen making big stock market splash.

text.p: High-speed Internet access provider At Home Corp. is poised to make its stock market debut Friday with a valuation of more than $1.2 billion as it rides the latest wave of investor euphoria over Web-related stocks.

Underwriter Morgan Stanley & Co. said late Thursday the offering was priced at $10.50 a share, towards the top of the upwardly revised range of $9 to $11 a share, and raised the number of shares to 9 million from 8 million.

The offering will raise $94.5 million in gross proceeds, prior to underwriters' fees. The company will have a total of 118.6 million shares outstanding, giving it a value of about $1.24 billion at the offering price.

Industry analysts and executives said At Home is poised to ride the rebound among the leading Internet companes -- with Internet search company Yahoo! Inc. and online bookseller Amazon.com surging to record highs this week.

By using so-called broadband cables and its own high speed network, the Redwood City, Calif.-based company is able to provide continous Internet access via cable modems at speeds more than 300 times faster than typical dial-up connections.

"I would not be surprised if it traded at $16 to $17," in its first trading session Friday, said Manish Shah, editor and publisher of the IPO Maven in New York. "The potential is certainly there in terms of significant traffic via cable."

At Home, which posted a net loss of about $24.5 million in 1996 on early deployment revenues of just $676,000 as it began service in several thousand homes, was initially funded in large part by major cable companies.

Investors include cable partners Tele-Communications Inc., Comcast Corp., Cox Communications Inc. and the venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers, and it recently added cable firms in Canada.

At Home's initial residential services have been rolled out to about 5,000 subscribers in 12 U.S. cities, and potential investors familiar with its plans said the company wants to raise this to about 400,000, or about 1 percent of the 44 million homes its cable partners pass, over the next several years.

At Home also provides business services, dubbed At Work, and it has been stepping up deployments in recent months and aims to cash in on frustration with the slow speed of Internet access over conventional phone lines.

Nevertheless, some potential investors raised concerns over At Home's dependence on its cable partners to deploy the system and over whether prices of $35 to $55 a month could be too costly to attract a mass market.

"The biggest problem the cable operators have is convincing the public that they are service oriented," said Shah. "But there is an exponential curve where it could be sustainable if they can attract, say, a million users."

Some industry executives working with the technology said At Home was providing just the sort of programming that will enable cable operators to deploy it with little fuss and that makes it easy for consumers to use.

"The market's beginning to recognize the potential of cable modems and Internet access to the home," said Henry Nicholas, chief executive officer of Irvine, Calif.-based Broadcom Corp., which provides computer chips for broadband communications. "This is going to be a huge market and I think At Home is very well positioned."

Like many other Internet companies, At Home said in a Securities and Exchange Commission filing in May for its initial public offering that it would face "substantial" operating and net losses in the near future.
At Home has not forecast when it will be profitable.
Along with Morgan Stanley, Merrill Lynch & Co., Alex. Brown & Sons Inc. and Hambrecht & Quist were underwriters.
